subtitulo: Stopped doing or stopped to do
descripcion: Some English verbs take a gerund, some take an infinitive, and a few change meaning depending on which one follows. At B2 the goal is to fix the most common verbs in each group and to know the handful (stop, remember, try) where the choice changes the meaning entirely.

filas: I enjoy reading in the evening.
I stopped smoking / I stopped to smoke.

ejemplos.texto: We decided to leave a bit earlier than planned.
I stopped checking my phone every five minutes.

notas: Stop + gerund means to quit a habit; stop + infinitive means to pause in order to do something else.
Remember + gerund is about a past memory; remember + infinitive is about not forgetting a future task.
After a preposition, English always uses the gerund: interested in learning, good at cooking.

contraste.es: Spanish uses the infinitive much more generally after almost any verb (decidí salir, disfruto leer), without the gerund–infinitive distinction English requires. Spanish speakers therefore default to the infinitive and avoid the gerund even where it is obligatory.
contraste.de: German has only the zu-infinitive after verbs, so German speakers default to the to-infinitive (I enjoy to read). A useful bridge is the German nominalised infinitive: das Lesen corresponds to the English gerund used as a noun (Reading is relaxing).
contraste.it: Italian uses the infinitive after prepositions (prima di uscire, senza dire niente), while English requires a gerund there. Italian speakers therefore produce before to go out or without say anything; the gerund after prepositions is the key point.
contraste.fr: French uses the infinitive after prepositions (avant de partir, sans rien dire, après avoir mangé), while English requires a gerund. This leads to before to leave, without to say anything or after to have eaten; the gerund after prepositions is the key point.
contraste.pt: Portuguese uses the infinitive after prepositions (antes de sair, sem dizer nada), and its gerúndio is a verb form, never a noun. This leads to before to leave and to Read is relaxing instead of Reading is relaxing.

errores: Using the infinitive after a preposition instead of the gerund.
Confusing stop + gerund and stop + infinitive.
Defaulting to the infinitive after verbs that require a gerund, like enjoy or avoid.

es: *para* + infinitive rendered as *for*: *I came for to learn* or *for learn* instead of *to learn*.
de: *um … zu* rendered as *for to*: *I save for to buy a car* instead of *to buy a car*.
it: *per* + infinitive rendered as *for*: *I study for learn* instead of *to learn*.
fr: *pour* + infinitive rendered as *for*: *I came for to see you* instead of *to see you*.
pt: *para* + infinitive rendered as *for*: *I study for learn* instead of *to learn*.

redemittel.funcion: checks the pairs where the form matters

mision.consigna: Write about how you recovered from an illness or injury.
requisitos: four verbs followed by a gerund
use *recovery*, *to take it easy* and *side effect*

microtareas.texto: Ten verbs: gerund or infinitive? Write one sentence each.
Two sentences with *stop -ing* and *stop to* about your *recovery*.
Record 90 seconds: what do you *enjoy doing* when you're ill?

autochequeo: Is the gerund used after every preposition?
Have I checked stop, remember and try for the intended meaning?
Does each verb take the correct form (gerund or infinitive)?
Have I avoided defaulting to the infinitive everywhere?
Are at least six different verb-plus-form combinations used?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on gerunds and infinitives. Check every preposition for a following gerund, and check stop, remember and try for their intended meaning. Do not rewrite the text.
